title: Prescribing for family
questionSheet: You are a prescribing pharmacist and the only pharmacist in a rural town in central Queensland. It is Saturday afternoon. Your wife, Xiaoyu, has developed symptoms of a urinary tract infection. The nearest other prescriber is a 3-hour drive away and is currently closed. Manage the situation as you would in practice.

notes: You are the only pharmacist in town.
Nearest alternate prescriber: 3-hour drive, currently closed.

patient.label: Xiaoyu (your wife)
patient.name: Xiaoyu
patient.description: The pharmacist's wife, in her thirties. Uncomfortable and keen to be treated today. She assumes her husband will just sort it out, and is a little surprised, though cooperative, when he treats it like a proper consultation.

bio.Full name: Xiaoyu Chen (you kept your own surname)

patient.situation: You have come into the pharmacy where your husband is the pharmacist, to ask him for help.
patient.openingLine: I think it's another UTI. Can you just give me something?
publicFacts: She has symptoms of a urinary tract infection: burning when she passes urine and needing to go often.
She would rather not drive three hours to another prescriber.

hiddenFacts.fact: No fever, no back or side pain, no nausea, and no blood in your urine. It started yesterday.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “Any fever, back or side pain, or blood in your urine? When did it start?”

hiddenFacts.fact: You are not pregnant and not breastfeeding. You have no allergies and take no regular medicines.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “Is there any chance you're pregnant? Any allergies or regular medicines?”

hiddenFacts.fact: Your last UTI was about two years ago and cleared up with a short course of antibiotics.
hiddenFacts.unlockHint: “Have you had a UTI before? When was the last one?”

answerKey.plantedProblem: Prescribing for a family member. The personal relationship may compromise, or appear to compromise, professional objectivity, set against timely access to treatment and antibiotic stewardship.
acceptableResolutions: Name the conflict with Integrity 3b and weigh it against the harm of delayed treatment.
Identify harms to her, to public trust in the profession, and to antibiotic stewardship.
With no timely alternative prescriber, prescribing can be justified if the assessment and decision stay objective and evidence-based.
Carry out a proper clinical assessment as for any patient, including red flags, pregnancy, allergies and history.
Document the indication, assessment, rationale, alternatives considered, guideline alignment and steps taken to minimise bias.
State that referral would be preferred if another prescriber were reasonably available.
unacceptableActions: Prescribing informally without an assessment or documentation.
Refusing all care without weighing the harm of delay.
Prescribing outside the guideline or protocol because she is family.
legal: Prescribe only within the Queensland pharmacist prescribing scope and protocol for uncomplicated UTI.
answerKey.modelAnswer: The dilemma is prescribing for a family member, where the relationship may undermine objectivity, set against timely treatment. Harms reach her, public trust and antibiotic stewardship. Referral keeps objectivity but would mean a 3-hour drive to a closed service. With no timely alternative, prescribing is justified when the assessment is complete and objective, the decision follows the protocol, and everything is documented: indication, assessment, rationale, alternatives and the steps taken to reduce bias. If another prescriber were reasonably available, referral would be the better option.
